name: Greater Israel
summary: Greater Israel (Eretz Yisrael HaShlema, the whole Land of Israel) is the position that the Jewish people hold a permanent national, and for religious adherents divinely given, right to the entire land between the Mediterranean and the Jordan, and in older Revisionist versions east of the Jordan too. Its adherents oppose partition, territorial concessions and a Palestinian state west of the Jordan, and treat Jewish settlement and Israeli sovereignty throughout the territory as a central national task. Secular Revisionists argue from national right and security behind an 'iron wall' of Jewish force, while religious Zionists in the tradition of the Kooks see holding and settling the land as part of redemption.
scope: Two strands that share the territorial core: (1) the secular Revisionist line of Ze'ev Jabotinsky, Herut and the Likud as reflected in the Iron Wall essay, the Revisionist and Herut programmes, the 1977 Likud platform and Begin's 1977 autonomy plan; and (2) the religious-settler line of Abraham Isaac Kook and Zvi Yehuda Kook, Gush Emunim, Tehiya and today's Religious Zionist party, including Bezalel Smotrich's 2017 'Decisive Plan' (read through a scholarly analysis that quotes it at length). Where these strands split (democracy versus divine command, the status of Arab residents, religion in public life, social questions) the answer is 0 or low confidence. It excludes the maximal Nile-to-Euphrates reading, the Kach movement's explicit transfer programme and the 1967 Labor-movement supporters of the Movement for Greater Israel, whose socialist economics differ. Economic answers follow the documented Revisionist/Herut positions and are mostly low or medium.

universal-healthcare.rationale: Herut, the main Revisionist party, paired its criticism of heavy state intervention with a call for a national health insurance system; the religious-settler strand has no distinct position.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Herut backed a legal minimum wage, but nothing in the Revisionist or settler sources calls for raising it substantially; inferred as neutral.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: The Revisionists favoured private initiative and private capital, and Herut called itself a liberal party that would block socialism; today's Religious Zionist party also generally backs free markets.

public-ownership.rationale: Inferred from the Revisionist preference for private capital and Herut's opposition to socialism; settlers themselves depend heavily on state funding, so the line is soft.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: No source states a position on taxing the rich; Herut mixed private-enterprise rhetoric with social legislation, so the answer is inferred as neutral.

unions-good.rationale: Inferred from the Revisionists' break with the Histadrut in 1934 and their call for compulsory arbitration; Herut later re-entered the Histadrut, and settler sources say nothing on unions.

property-fundamental.rationale: Revisionists favoured private property, but the settlement project rests on registering contested land as state land, so a strong property right is not a principle the doctrine applies; inferred.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Neither strand addresses corporate regulation; the Religious Zionist party mixes deregulation with breaking up monopolies and a bank-profits tax, so inferred as neutral.

cut-welfare.rationale: Herut sought working-class votes with social legislation while praising private enterprise; no source treats welfare as dependency, so the answer is inferred.

worker-ownership.rationale: Inferred from the Revisionist criticism of collective (kibbutz-style) settlement as a drain on capital competing with the private economy.

surveillance-ok.rationale: Inferred from the doctrine's security framing of the territories and its pledge to eliminate armed Palestinian organisations; no source discusses surveillance.

legalize-drugs.rationale: Inferred from the religious strand's emphasis on the state's Jewish character; no Revisionist or settler source discusses drug policy.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: No source addresses hate-speech law; Revisionist liberalism and the settler right's own legal clashes leave no clear answer, so inferred as neutral.

strong-leader.rationale: Revisionism relied heavily on leaders (Jabotinsky, Begin), but Jabotinsky and Herut worked through parliament; inferred as neutral.

state-harmful.rationale: Zvi Yehuda Kook told his students that the State of Israel is the state the prophets foresaw, a stage of redemption, and Revisionism's aim was a sovereign Jewish state; both strands treat the state as sacred or essential.

limit-guns.rationale: Inferred from settler practice of arming regional security committees and Jabotinsky's stress on Jewish self-defence; no source discusses civilian gun law as such.

empower-police-military.rationale: The Iron Wall doctrine makes armed force the precondition of settlement, and later platforms pledge to destroy armed Palestinian organisations, so adherents favour strong security forces.

legalize-sex-work.rationale: Inferred from the religious strand's emphasis on Jewish tradition and family values; Revisionist sources are silent.

decide-locally.rationale: Inferred: the doctrine is about national sovereignty over the whole land, decided centrally; settler regional councils are a tool of that aim, not a localist principle.

rehabilitation.rationale: No source discusses penal policy; inferred as neutral.

traditional-family.rationale: The religious-settler parties campaign on family values; secular Revisionist sources say nothing, so the answer is inferred from one strand.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: The Religious Zionist alliance has opposed recognising same-sex marriage, while secular Likud adherents vary; strands are split.

abortion-legal.rationale: Religious settlers lean against abortion while the secular Revisionist tradition is silent; strands are split.

more-religion-public.rationale: Religious Zionists want a stronger Jewish character of the state, and the NZO aimed to implant Jewish tradition in Jewish life, though Jabotinsky said the religious question was secondary; inferred mild agreement.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Inferred: the doctrine treats the Jewish return as rectifying Jewish homelessness and rejects Palestinian historical claims, so it would not frame policy as correcting injustices against Arabs.

gender-social-construct.rationale: Inferred from the religious strand's traditionalism; the doctrine does not address gender theory.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: The NZO aimed to revive the Jewish state and language and implant Jewish tradition, and the Religious Zionist party campaigns on strengthening the state's Jewish character.

gradual-change.rationale: Inferred: Gush Emunim created irreversible facts on the ground ahead of government decisions and the Revisionists demanded immediate statehood, so neither strand prizes gradualism.

reduce-immigration.rationale: The doctrine encourages Jewish immigration and settlement; for non-Jewish immigration there is no stated position, so the answer leans on Jewish immigration and is inferred.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: The 1977 Likud platform rejects solutions invented by outsiders and insists on direct negotiation with no preconditions, which implies resistance to empowering international bodies over Israel's borders.

free-trade.rationale: Revisionists combined private enterprise with state protection of local industry during state-building, so the answer on free trade is inferred as neutral.

nation-first.rationale: Platforms put the Jewish people's eternal right to the land above outside peace proposals and reject externally designed solutions.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: No source discusses intervention abroad for human rights; inferred as neutral.

open-borders.rationale: The doctrine is about fixing and holding national borders at the Jordan, and settler programmes reject any second national movement west of it, which is incompatible with open borders.

limit-growth.rationale: Inferred from the settlement project's emphasis on building towns, infrastructure and hundreds of thousands of new residents.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: Not part of either strand's programme; inferred as neutral.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: No source addresses technology and progress; inferred as neutral.

expand-nuclear.rationale: No source addresses nuclear power; inferred as neutral.

revolution-justified.rationale: Begin's Irgun, from the Revisionist camp, waged armed revolt against British rule, though Jabotinsky preferred legal pressure; strands and periods are split.

experts-over-public.rationale: Inferred from the settler right's push to curb the attorney-general and the courts in favour of elected ministers.

central-planning.rationale: Revisionists favoured private capital with minimal state involvement and Herut pledged to block any attempt to establish socialism.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: No source addresses environmental ethics; inferred as neutral.

limit-population.rationale: Inferred: the doctrine seeks to increase the Jewish population of the land through immigration and settlement.

missingStatements.text: A state should apply its full sovereignty to territory it controls and claims as part of its homeland, rather than leave it under military administration or negotiate its future status.
missingStatements.rationale: Asserting sovereignty over Judea and Samaria is the doctrine's programme, from the 1977 Likud platform to Tehiya's annexation demand and Smotrich's call to impose sovereignty on all of it.
missingStatements.declined: Statement bank frozen on 2026-10-22, before the people audits: no new statements are added.

notes: Strands that would answer differently: Jabotinsky's own liberal minority-rights programme (equal citizenship, national-cultural autonomy) versus Smotrich's residency-without-citizenship and encouraged emigration; Revisionist parliamentary legalism versus Gush Emunim's view that the land cannot be surrendered even by an elected government. The 1967 Movement for Greater Israel also drew Labor-movement figures (Tabenkin, Alterman) with socialist economics, excluded here. Two sources (s15, s17) are critical commentary and s6 is a Palestinian research centre's analysis; they are used for what they quote or report, not their framing.
